chapter: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
title: Recording the band in a speakeasy in 1950
summary: Bergen recalls the band being recorded on the floor of a bar with an out-of-tune piano and Donald Sewer, and the tape being reused.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And I'll never forget you boys were recording my band and we had the recorder set up in the middle of the floor and some girl that Dutch knew, she got mad. She raised the devil because we were right in the middle of the floor without recording apparatus, but they didn't have anybody in there hardly. I don't see why we were offending them. Maybe they figured somebody might come in and want to dance and think they were not operating. But that piano was so badly out of tune Dick, it wasn't too good. And I think they had an exhaust fan in there. If you still have that tape or a record from it, you could almost hear a little fast vibration and Donald Sewer's notes on it. But that was back in 1950.
Bob Greenwood I think had the tape machine.

Oh Bobby, yeah. Bobby was there because we had a playback on it. But I think I gave all those records away I believe. The tape, I finally erased the tape and I still have part of it backwards. You know how you splice the tape backwards? As I told you, that's where I think that the patents for the original Bob came from. So they ran the tape backwards and they got the licks off, I'd say, and they used that timing. I really do believe it. Now Dick, I think we were up to 50, 1955, we were still in the union, playing spot jobs. Of course I met a lot of fire musicians, played with all the old timers. And up until about 65 everything was going good. And then I had a lot of teeth pulled. I might as well tell the public this because some of them know it. But I didn't realize my trouble was messing teeth back here. I started thinking that I had a bad mouthpiece, which was very stupid of me, after playing on a mouthpiece a few years. And I started changing mouthpieces. I went from bed. In two weeks I couldn't hardly play. I couldn't get a sound at the heart. And it took me about three years to realize that I had to tighten up twice as hard on the right side of my mouth because there's nothing, no vibration, no foundation for these muscles to rest on. You lost your back molar.
